title: Matot: keep your word (Numbers 30:3)
hook: whatever a person vows, they shall do

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tamid, two lambs a day, morning and evening, became the rhythm of daily prayer. Your line was morning and evening. Did you keep your two small anchors? Day four hundred seventy-one.

I'll call you back. Let's get lunch sometime. I'll definitely be there. These get said all the time, and some of them quietly evaporate. Nobody keeps score, mostly. A new portion begins today, Matot, and it opens with Moses speaking not to the whole people but to the heads of the tribes, the leaders. The first subject he raises isn't war or land. It's the words that come out of our mouths, and whether they mean anything.
screen: `I'LL CALL YOU BACK.` → `MATOT: THE HEADS OF THE TRIBES.` → `THE WORDS OUT OF OUR MOUTHS.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse. When a man makes a vow to the Lord, or swears an oath to bind himself, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "he shall not break his word; he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth." The word for vow is neder: a promise that binds you, often to give something, or to do or not do something. The phrase for break his word, in Hebrew, is lo yachel devaro. Rashi links yachel to a root that means making something ordinary, profane. Don't make your words common. Don't let them become cheap. The chapter then goes on through cases: when a vow stands, and when, in that ancient household, a father or husband could cancel one on the day he heard it. The Torah takes spoken words so seriously that it needs rules for undoing them. And precisely because a vow is so binding, the later tradition grew cautious about making them at all. The book of Ecclesiastes says, in paraphrase, better not to vow than to vow and not pay. Some Jews, when they promise something small, add two words: bli neder. Without a vow. I'll be there Thursday, bli neder. It doesn't mean they don't intend to come. It means they know how heavy a real promise is, and they won't make one lightly. And on the eve of Yom Kippur, the service opens with Kol Nidre, a formula about vows. The Day of Atonement begins with the words we've said.
screen: `NEDER: A VOW THAT BINDS.` · `DON'T MAKE YOUR WORDS COMMON.` · `BETTER NOT TO VOW THAN TO BREAK IT.` · `BLI NEDER: WITHOUT A VOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one small promise today. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last week. What did you say you'd do, casually, that you haven't done yet? A call, a text, returning something, an hour of help. Pick just one. Picture the person who heard you say it. Now decide when, today, you'll keep it: the exact moment. Let your word become solid again. Breathe with that decision until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Neder. A vow, a binding promise. The Torah says: whoever vows shall not break his word, but do all that comes out of his mouth.
Your line: keep your word. Today, before you say I'll do it, pause; then keep the promise you choose to make. Day four hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Some Jews add 'bli neder', without a vow, to everyday promises so that an ordinary intention isn't taken as a binding vow, and Yom Kippur eve opens with Kol Nidre, a formula concerning vows.

original.note: Hebrew: a vow; the plural, nedarim, is also the name of a Talmud tractate about vows.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old rule about religious promises.
what it means: what you say binds you, so don't let your words become cheap.
what a scholar hears: Rashi links lo yachel devaro to chol, the ordinary or profane: don't make your words common; Ecclesiastes 5:4 warns it's better not to vow.

notes: Numbers 30:3 (JPS numbering; 30:2 in KJV): confirm JPS 1917 wording of the quoted clause.
Rashi on 30:3: 'lo yachel' as 'shall not make his word chullin (profane)'; confirm.
The annulment rules for a daughter's or wife's vows (30:4–17) are mentioned briefly and descriptively; a Keeper may want different framing.
Kol Nidre is described only as 'a formula about vows'; its exact function (annulment of future/past vows) differs by rite.
